clinicalPearls: A slow-growing thermophilic scotochromogen that grows optimally at high temperatures (around 42 to 45 degrees Celsius)
Its thermophilia explains its niche in hot-water systems, including hospital water supplies, storage tanks, and taps
Contaminated water and bronchoscopes have caused pseudo-outbreaks, so isolation does not always indicate true disease
Most often causes chronic cavitary or fibronodular upper-lobe pulmonary disease in middle-aged men with pre-existing lung disease
Distinguishing genuine infection from colonisation or laboratory pseudo-infection requires careful application of diagnostic criteria
Recovery in the laboratory is improved by incubating cultures at a higher temperature
Treatment usually combines rifampicin, ethambutol, and a macrolide, sometimes with a quinolone, though the optimal regimen is uncertain and outcomes are guarded
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium xenopi is a slow-growing, thermophilic scotochromogenic mycobacterium that thrives in hot-water systems, its principal reservoir. Inhalation of aerosols leads to pulmonary infection predominantly in hosts with structural lung disease, producing cavitary or fibronodular changes. Because the organism colonises water systems and instruments, it is frequently isolated as a contaminant or coloniser, and clusters of positive cultures may represent pseudo-outbreaks rather than disease. Disseminated infection is uncommon and occurs with significant immunosuppression. Reported mortality is relatively high, though this partly reflects the burden of underlying comorbidity.

redFlags: Progressive cavitary disease with weight loss or haemoptysis
Clustered isolates suggesting a contaminated water source or bronchoscope needing investigation
Deterioration despite therapy given the guarded response
reference.prognosis: The prognosis of M. xenopi pulmonary disease is guarded, with relatively high mortality that is influenced strongly by coexisting lung disease and comorbidity. Response to treatment is variable and the best regimen remains uncertain, so outcomes are less favourable than for M. kansasii.
pitfalls: Treating a contaminant or coloniser as genuine disease without meeting diagnostic criteria
Overlooking a contaminated hospital water supply or bronchoscope in clustered cases
Failing to incubate cultures at a higher temperature, reducing recovery
Attributing all clinical decline to the organism rather than to underlying comorbidity

management: Treat with prolonged multidrug combination therapy, typically rifampicin and ethambutol with a macrolide and/or a fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin, accepting that the optimal regimen remains uncertain
Distinguish genuine disease from colonisation or laboratory pseudo-infection through repeated respiratory cultures and strict diagnostic criteria before treating
Ask the laboratory to incubate cultures at a higher temperature to improve recovery of this thermophilic organism
Consider surgical resection for localised cavitary disease in suitable candidates as an adjunct to drug therapy
Manage the underlying lung disease and coexisting comorbidity, which strongly influence outcome
Investigate hospital hot-water systems and bronchoscope decontamination when clustered isolates suggest a pseudo-outbreak
Refer to infectious diseases or respiratory medicine, recognising the guarded prognosis and relatively high mortality
